disease.disease_name: Pompe Disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II)
disease.mechanism: Loss-of-function. Deficiency of lysosomal alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase) impairs lysosomal glycogen degradation, causing glycogen to accumulate in lysosomes, especially in skeletal and cardiac muscle. This causes progressive muscle weakness, respiratory failure, and (in the infantile form) severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
disease.autotac_rationale: NOT eligible. Pompe disease is a loss-of-function enzyme deficiency — acid alpha-glucosidase is deficient, not accumulated. Correct route is enzyme replacement therapy (restore GAA), not protein degradation.
disease.prevalence: ~1 in 40,000 (all forms combined); infantile form ~1 in 138,000 — commonly cited; UNVERIFIED exact figure this session
disease.age_of_onset: Infantile onset (0-12 months, severe cardiomyopathy) or late-onset (childhood/adult, muscle weakness)

approved_treatments.mechanism_correct: Recombinant acid alpha-glucosidase that replaces the deficient enzyme, restoring lysosomal glycogen degradation. Administered intravenously every 2 weeks. Disease-modifying for both infantile and late-onset forms.
approved_treatments.note: NOTE: alglucosidase alfa is a recombinant glycoprotein enzyme (~110 kDa), NOT a small molecule — MW/PubChem CID left 0 to avoid fabrication.

investigational: Next-generation ERT: avalglucosidase alfa (Nexviazyme) — improved M6P targeting

disease.human_summary: Pompe disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency, leading to glycogen accumulation in muscle. The infantile form causes severe cardiomyopathy and early death; the late-onset form causes progressive muscle weakness and respiratory failure. Enzyme replacement therapy is the standard disease-modifying treatment.
